problem_statement:
Core Erlang compilation target
## Goal

Add a Core Erlang compilation target alongside the existing Erlang abstract-forms path (`af_word_compiler.erl`, `af_ring1.erl` native mode), selectable per-compile.

## Motivation

- Core Erlang is the compiler's intermediate representation. Generating it directly gives finer control over the emitted code than abstract forms allow.
- Some optimizations (case transformations, inline expansion, better TCO visibility) are natural in Core but awkward in abstract forms.
- Keeps the door open for non-BEAM targets that consume Core (e.g., Lumen-style projects).

## Scope

Feature parity with the abstract-forms path for:
- Stack operations, arithmetic, comparison, logic
- Multi-clause functions with value-constraint patterns in heads
- Product types (constructor, getters, setters)
- Inter-word calls within and across modules
- Actor primitives (spawn/send/receive)
- List, map, string, tuple operations
- FFI calls

## Files expected to add/change

- New: `src/af_core_compiler.erl` (generates `cerl:c_module/4` trees)
- Changes to `src/af_ring1.erl` to support a new mode `{mode, core}` alongside `interp`/`native`
- Tests in `test/af_core_compiler_tests.erl` mirroring the existing BEAM tests

## Acceptance

- Every test that currently runs against native BEAM also runs against Core-generated BEAM with identical outputs
- `compile-to-core` word (or similar) in `af_type_beam.erl` exposes the path to user code
- Unit tests >=95% coverage on new code
- Documentation note in `docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` describing when to prefer core vs abstract-forms

## Risk

This is the largest item on this batch. May deliver in stages (core for stack + arithmetic first, then multi-clause, then product types, etc.). Each stage lands behind a feature flag so `native` remains the default.

### Additional contract requirements

# Core Erlang target: module `af_core_target` (public contract)

This delivery is the first stage of the Core Erlang compilation target. It
introduces a new public module, `src/af_core_target.erl`, that turns word
definitions (lists of `#operation{}` records from `include/operation.hrl`)
into Core Erlang and compiles them to loadable BEAM code. The stage is
intentionally bounded: only the primitives and literal forms listed below
are accepted, and the wider feature-parity scope described in the problem
statement is not part of this stage.

## Stack convention

Stacks are represented as lists whose head is the top of the stack
(TOS-first). Compiled words are unary functions taking one stack list and
returning the updated stack list. Values on the stack are `{TypeName,
Value}` tuples, so an integer on the stack looks like `{'Int', 5}`.
Binary arithmetic is computed in Forth order: for input stack containing
`b` on top and `a` underneath, `+`/`-`/`*`/`/` compute `a OP b` (for
example, `[{'Int',3},{'Int',10}]` with `-` yields `[{'Int',7}]`).
Operations deeper in the stack (the "rest") are preserved unchanged.

## Exported functions

### `supported_primitives() -> [string()]`

Returns the names of the primitive operations this target can compile.
The list contains at least `"dup"`, `"drop"`, `"swap"`, `"+"`, `"-"`,
`"*"`, and `"/"`. Integer literals (an operation whose name parses as an
integer, e.g. `"42"`) are also accepted as push operations even though
they are not included in the returned list.

### `compile_word(Name, SigIn, SigOut, Body) -> {ok, CerlFunPair} | {error, Reason}`

* `Name :: string()` — word name; `SigIn`, `SigOut :: [atom()]` —
  signatures (`SigOut` is informational for this stage); `Body ::
  [#operation{}]` — the word body.
* Validates the body and compiles it. An empty body is valid and accepted.
* Returns `{error, {unsupported_primitive, OpName}}` (or an equivalent
  informative error tuple whose textual rendering contains the offending
  operation name) when the body uses an unsupported primitive.
* Returns `{error, Reason}` for any other failure; malformed inputs that
  raise unexpected exceptions are caught and reported as an error tuple
  rather than crashing the caller.

### `compile_words_to_binary(ModName, WordDefs) -> {ok, ModName, Binary} | {error, Reason}`

* `ModName :: atom()`, `WordDefs :: [{Name :: string(), SigIn ::
  [atom()], SigOut :: [atom()], Body :: [#operation{}]}]`.
* Compiles all given word definitions into one module and returns the
  BEAM binary without loading it. Each word is exported as a 1-arity
  function named by its word name, callable as `ModName:Word(Stack)`.
* Any unsupported primitive in any word aborts the whole compilation with
  an error that identifies the offending operation; no binary is returned.

### `compile_words_to_module(ModName, WordDefs) -> {ok, ModName} | {error, Reason}`

* Same inputs and word semantics as `compile_words_to_binary/2`, but the
  resulting module is immediately loaded, so its words can be invoked
  right away as `ModName:Word(Stack)`.
* Compilation errors propagate from `compile_words_to_binary/2` and are
  returned as `{error, Reason}`.

## End-to-end semantics

After a successful `compile_words_to_module/2`, calling a generated word
applies its operation sequence to the supplied stack:

* `dup` duplicates the top stack item; `drop` removes it; `swap`
  exchanges the top two items.
* `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` pop the top two integer items and push their
  combined integer result (Forth order as above); `/` performs integer
  division.
* An integer literal pushes `{'Int', N}` onto the stack.
* Multiple words may be compiled into one module and are independently
  callable.
* A binary produced by `compile_words_to_binary/2` is loadable with
  `code:load_binary/3` and behaves identically once loaded.

diff --git a/src/af_core_target.erl b/src/af_core_target.erl
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..5e1db05
--- /dev/null
+++ b/src/af_core_target.erl
@@ -0,0 +1,212 @@
+%% af_core_target.erl -- Core Erlang compilation target
+%%
+%% Experimental alternative to af_word_compiler's Erlang abstract-forms path.
+%% Emits Core Erlang (cerl AST) directly, compiled via `compile:forms/2`
+%% with the `from_core` option.
+%%
+%% Status (v1): MVP subset. Supports stack operations (dup, drop, swap),
+%% arithmetic (+, -, *, /), Int literals, and single-clause word definitions.
+%% Does NOT support multi-clause dispatch, product types, actors, FFI, or
+%% most collection ops. Words using unsupported primitives will be rejected
+%% with {error, {unsupported_primitive, Name}}.
+%%
+%% Motivation: Core Erlang gives finer control over the emitted IR than the
+%% existing abstract-forms backend. Some optimisations (case coalescing,
+%% inline expansion, better TCO visibility) are natural in Core but awkward
+%% in abstract forms. This module lays the groundwork; full feature parity
+%% with af_word_compiler is a future effort.
+
+-module(af_core_target).
+
+-include("operation.hrl").
+
+-export([compile_word/4, compile_words_to_module/2, compile_words_to_binary/2]).
+-export([supported_primitives/0]).
+
+%%====================================================================
+%% Public API
+%%====================================================================
+
+%% compile_word(Name, SigIn, SigOut, Body) -> {ok, Cerl} | {error, Reason}
+%%
+%% Compile a single word definition to a Core Erlang function definition.
+%% Returns a {FNameCerl, FunCerl} pair suitable for inclusion in a module.
+compile_word(Name, SigIn, _SigOut, Body) ->
+    try
+        case validate_body(Body) of
+            ok ->
+                FName = cerl:c_fname(list_to_atom(Name), 1),
+                Arg   = cerl:c_var('_Stack'),
+                BodyCerl = build_body(SigIn, Body),
+                Fun   = cerl:c_fun([Arg], BodyCerl),
+                {ok, {FName, wrap_with_destructure(Arg, SigIn, Fun)}};
+            {error, _} = Err -> Err
+        end
+    catch
+        throw:ThrownReason -> {error, ThrownReason};
+        Class:Reason -> {error, {Class, Reason}}
+    end.
+
+%% compile_words_to_module(ModName, WordDefs) -> {ok, ModName} | {error, Reason}
+%%
+%% Compile and load a module.
+compile_words_to_module(ModName, WordDefs) when is_atom(ModName) ->
+    case compile_words_to_binary(ModName, WordDefs) of
+        {ok, ModName, Binary} ->
+            code:load_binary(ModName, atom_to_list(ModName) ++ ".beam", Binary),
+            {ok, ModName};
+        {error, _} = Err -> Err
+    end.
+
+%% compile_words_to_binary(ModName, WordDefs) -> {ok, ModName, Binary} | {error, Reason}
+%%
+%% WordDefs = [{Name, SigIn, SigOut, Body}, ...]
+compile_words_to_binary(ModName, WordDefs) when is_atom(ModName) ->
+    try
+        Defs = lists:map(fun({Name, SigIn, SigOut, Body}) ->
+            case compile_word(Name, SigIn, SigOut, Body) of
+                {ok, Pair} -> Pair;
+                {error, Reason} -> throw({compile_error, Name, Reason})
+            end
+        end, WordDefs),
+        Exports = [FName || {FName, _} <- Defs],
+        ModCerl = cerl:c_module(
+            cerl:c_atom(ModName),
+            Exports,
+            [],
+            Defs
+        ),
+        case compile:forms(ModCerl, [from_core, binary, return_errors]) of
+            {ok, ModName, Bin} -> {ok, ModName, Bin};
+            {ok, ModName, Bin, _Warnings} -> {ok, ModName, Bin};
+            {error, Errs, _Warns} -> {error, {core_compile, Errs}};
+            error -> {error, core_compile_failed}
+        end
+    catch
+        throw:Reason -> {error, Reason}
+    end.
+
+%% supported_primitives/0 -> [string()]
+%%
+%% List of primitive names this target currently handles. Useful for tooling
+%% that wants to pre-filter word definitions before attempting compilation.
+supported_primitives() ->
+    ["dup", "drop", "swap", "+", "-", "*", "/"].
+
+%%====================================================================
+%% Body validation
+%%====================================================================
+
+validate_body([]) -> ok;
+validate_body([#operation{name = Name} | Rest]) ->
+    case is_supported_primitive(Name) orelse parse_int_literal(Name) =/= error of
+        true -> validate_body(Rest);
+        false -> {error, {unsupported_primitive, Name}}
+    end.
+
+is_supported_primitive(Name) ->
+    lists:member(Name, supported_primitives()).
+
+%%====================================================================
+%% Body construction
+%%====================================================================
+
+%% build_body(SigIn, Body) -> cerl()
+%%
+%% Emit a Core Erlang expression that represents the word body. The input
+%% stack is bound to the variable '_Stack' (see compile_word). The body is
+%% built as a fold that threads an "abstract stack" of cerl expressions.
+build_body(SigIn, Body) ->
+    %% Destructure the input sig into concrete cerl vars, then interpret
+    %% body ops against that cerl stack.
+    {Vars, RestVar} = destructure_vars(SigIn),
+    Destructured = cerl:make_list(Vars, cerl:c_var(RestVar)),
+    InputMatch = cerl:c_var('_Stack'),
+    CaseClause = cerl:c_clause([Destructured],
+                                 interpret_body(Vars, RestVar, Body)),
+    cerl:c_case(InputMatch, [CaseClause]).
+
+wrap_with_destructure(_Arg, _SigIn, Fun) ->
+    %% Destructuring is folded into the body's case expression, so the fun
+    %% itself is just fun(_Stack) -> case _Stack of ... end end.
+    Fun.
+
+destructure_vars(SigIn) ->
+    %% Bind a cerl variable for each sig_in entry. Order is TOS-first
+    %% (index 0 = TOS) matching the af_type convention.
+    Vars = [cerl:c_var(list_to_atom("_V" ++ integer_to_list(I)))
+            || I <- lists:seq(0, length(SigIn) - 1)],
+    %% Each var actually binds the {Type, Value} tuple.
+    Tuples = [cerl:make_list(
+                [cerl:c_var(list_to_atom("_V" ++ integer_to_list(I)))], cerl:c_nil())
+              || I <- lists:seq(0, length(SigIn) - 1)],
+    _ = Tuples,
+    {Vars, '_Rest'}.
+
+interpret_body(Vars, RestVar, Body) ->
+    %% Starting stack: the tagged {Type, Value} tuples one per var, TOS first.
+    InitStack = [cerl:c_var(cerl:var_name(V)) || V <- Vars],
+    FinalStack = lists:foldl(fun(Op, Stack) ->
+        apply_op(Op, Stack)
+    end, InitStack, Body),
+    rebuild_list(FinalStack, RestVar).
+
+apply_op(#operation{name = "dup"}, [Top | Rest]) ->
+    [Top, Top | Rest];
+apply_op(#operation{name = "drop"}, [_ | Rest]) ->
+    Rest;
+apply_op(#operation{name = "swap"}, [A, B | Rest]) ->
+    [B, A | Rest];
+apply_op(#operation{name = "+"}, Stack) -> binop('+', Stack);
+apply_op(#operation{name = "-"}, Stack) -> binop('-', Stack);
+apply_op(#operation{name = "*"}, Stack) -> binop('*', Stack);
+apply_op(#operation{name = "/"}, Stack) -> binop('div', Stack);
+apply_op(#operation{name = Name}, Stack) ->
+    case parse_int_literal(Name) of
+        {ok, N} ->
+            Lit = cerl:c_tuple([cerl:c_atom('Int'), cerl:c_int(N)]),
+            [Lit | Stack];
+        error ->
+            throw({unsupported_primitive, Name})
+    end.
+
+binop(Op, [B, A | Rest]) ->
+    %% Stack is TOS-first: top was pushed last. For `a b -`: a - b.
+    AVal = extract_int(A),
+    BVal = extract_int(B),
+    Sum = cerl:c_call(cerl:c_atom(erlang), cerl:c_atom(Op), [AVal, BVal]),
+    Tup = cerl:c_tuple([cerl:c_atom('Int'), Sum]),
+    [Tup | Rest].
+
+%% Extract the integer value from a {Int, N} tagged tuple expression.
+%% Works for both literal tuples we built and variables referring to input
+%% {Int, X} cells.
+extract_int(Expr) ->
+    case cerl:is_c_tuple(Expr) of
+        true ->
+            %% It's a literal {Int, N} we constructed. Grab element 2.
+            [_TypeAtom, ValExpr] = cerl:tuple_es(Expr),
+            ValExpr;
+        false ->
+            %% It's a variable; project element 2 via erlang:element/2.
+            cerl:c_call(cerl:c_atom(erlang), cerl:c_atom(element),
+                        [cerl:c_int(2), Expr])
+    end.
+
+%% Rebuild the Erlang list representation of the stack from cerl expressions.
+rebuild_list(Stack, RestVar) ->
+    %% Each element of `Stack` is either a cerl var referring to a
+    %% {Type, Value} tuple (passed through) or a fresh cerl tuple we built.
+    Elems = lists:map(fun lift_stack_item/1, Stack),
+    cerl:make_list(Elems, cerl:c_var(RestVar)).
+
+lift_stack_item(Expr) ->
+    case cerl:is_c_tuple(Expr) of
+        true -> Expr;
+        false -> Expr  %% variable: already a tuple at runtime
+    end.
+
+parse_int_literal(Str) ->
+    try {ok, list_to_integer(Str)}
+    catch _:_ -> error
+    end.

diff --git a/test/af_core_target_tests.erl b/test/af_core_target_tests.erl
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..d64cd6b
--- /dev/null
+++ b/test/af_core_target_tests.erl
@@ -0,0 +1,237 @@
+-module(af_core_target_tests).
+
+-include_lib("eunit/include/eunit.hrl").
+-include("operation.hrl").
+
+%% Build a minimal #operation{} that references a primitive by name. The
+%% Core Erlang target does not need an impl — it works off the name alone.
+op(Name) ->
+    #operation{name = Name, sig_in = [], sig_out = [],
+               impl = undefined, source = undefined}.
+
+setup() ->
+    af_type:reset().
+
+%%====================================================================
+%% supported_primitives/0
+%%====================================================================
+
+supported_primitives_test_() ->
+    Sup = af_core_target:supported_primitives(),
+    [
+        ?_assert(lists:member("dup", Sup)),
+        ?_assert(lists:member("drop", Sup)),
+        ?_assert(lists:member("swap", Sup)),
+        ?_assert(lists:member("+", Sup)),
+        ?_assert(lists:member("-", Sup)),
+        ?_assert(lists:member("*", Sup)),
+        ?_assert(lists:member("/", Sup))
+    ].
+
+%%====================================================================
+%% Validation rejects unsupported primitives
+%%====================================================================
+
+validation_test_() ->
+    [
+        {"compile_word accepts supported body", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("dup"), op("+")],
+            R = af_core_target:compile_word("double", ['Int'], ['Int'], Body),
+            ?assertMatch({ok, _}, R)
+        end},
+
+        {"compile_word rejects unsupported primitive", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("map-new")],
+            R = af_core_target:compile_word("bad", [], ['Map'], Body),
+            %% Must fail with an informative error that names the offending op.
+            ?assertMatch({error, _}, R),
+            {error, Reason} = R,
+            ?assert(string:str(lists:flatten(io_lib:format("~p", [Reason])), "map-new") > 0)
+        end},
+
+        {"empty body is accepted", fun() ->
+            R = af_core_target:compile_word("noop", [], [], []),
+            ?assertMatch({ok, _}, R)
+        end}
+    ].
+
+%%====================================================================
+%% End-to-end: compile and run
+%%====================================================================
+
+compile_and_run_test_() ->
+    {foreach, fun setup/0, fun(_) -> ok end, [
+        fun(_) -> {"double via Core Erlang", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("dup"), op("+")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_double,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"double", ['Int'], ['Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            %% Invoke the generated function
+            Result = ModName:double([{'Int', 5}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 10}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"double preserves rest of stack", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("dup"), op("+")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_double_rest,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"double", ['Int'], ['Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            Result = ModName:double([{'Int', 3}, {'Int', 99}, {'Bool', true}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 6}, {'Int', 99}, {'Bool', true}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"subtract via Core Erlang", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("-")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_sub,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"sub", ['Int', 'Int'], ['Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            %% Stack: [a, b] (TOS-first means b is top). For `a b -` we want a - b.
+            %% Our caller passes TOS-first: [TOP, UNDER, ...].
+            %% The compiler destructures TOS=V0, under=V1. For "-" we compute
+            %% V1 - V0 (under minus top), matching Forth convention.
+            Result = ModName:sub([{'Int', 3}, {'Int', 10}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 7}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"multiply via Core Erlang", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("*")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_mul,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"mul", ['Int', 'Int'], ['Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            Result = ModName:mul([{'Int', 7}, {'Int', 6}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 42}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"integer division via Core Erlang", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("/")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_div,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"divide", ['Int', 'Int'], ['Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            Result = ModName:divide([{'Int', 3}, {'Int', 15}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 5}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"drop via Core Erlang", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("drop")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_drop,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"dropit", ['Int'], [], Body}]
+            ),
+            Result = ModName:dropit([{'Int', 99}, {'Int', 7}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 7}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"swap via Core Erlang", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("swap")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_swap,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"swp", ['Int', 'Int'], ['Int', 'Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            Result = ModName:swp([{'Int', 1}, {'Int', 2}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 2}, {'Int', 1}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"int literal push via Core Erlang", fun() ->
+            %% Body with literal "42" op pushes {Int, 42}
+            Body = [op("42")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_lit,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"push42", [], ['Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            Result = ModName:push42([]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 42}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"literal plus add", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("dup"), op("1"), op("+")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_addone,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [{"incdup", ['Int'], ['Int', 'Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            Result = ModName:incdup([{'Int', 5}]),
+            %% dup 5 -> [5, 5]
+            %% 1 -> [1, 5, 5]
+            %% + -> [6, 5]  (top+under)
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 6}, {'Int', 5}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"compile_words_to_binary returns a loadable binary", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("dup"), op("+")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_bin,
+            {ok, ModName, Bin} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_binary(
+                ModName,
+                [{"double", ['Int'], ['Int'], Body}]
+            ),
+            ?assert(is_binary(Bin)),
+            %% Load it manually
+            {module, ModName} = code:load_binary(
+                ModName, atom_to_list(ModName) ++ ".beam", Bin),
+            Result = ModName:double([{'Int', 4}]),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 8}], Result)
+        end} end,
+
+        fun(_) -> {"multiple words in one module", fun() ->
+            DoubleBody = [op("dup"), op("+")],
+            SquareBody = [op("dup"), op("*")],
+            ModName = af_core_test_multi,
+            {ok, ModName} = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                ModName,
+                [
+                    {"double", ['Int'], ['Int'], DoubleBody},
+                    {"square", ['Int'], ['Int'], SquareBody}
+                ]
+            ),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 10}], ModName:double([{'Int', 5}])),
+            ?assertEqual([{'Int', 25}], ModName:square([{'Int', 5}]))
+        end} end
+    ]}.
+
+%%====================================================================
+%% Error cases
+%%====================================================================
+
+error_paths_test_() ->
+    [
+        {"unsupported primitive surfaces in compile_words_to_binary", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("map-new")],
+            R = af_core_target:compile_words_to_binary(
+                af_core_test_err,
+                [{"bad", [], [], Body}]
+            ),
+            %% Must fail with an informative error naming the offending op.
+            ?assertMatch({error, _}, R),
+            {error, Reason} = R,
+            ?assert(string:str(lists:flatten(io_lib:format("~p", [Reason])), "map-new") > 0)
+        end},
+
+        {"compile_words_to_module propagates binary errors", fun() ->
+            Body = [op("map-new")],
+            R = af_core_target:compile_words_to_module(
+                af_core_test_module_err,
+                [{"bad", [], [], Body}]
+            ),
+            ?assertMatch({error, _}, R)
+        end},
+
+        {"compile_word catches unexpected exceptions", fun() ->
+            %% Pass a non-list body. validate_body/1's pattern match on
+            %% [] | [_|_] will fail (function_clause) so the generic
+            %% catch in compile_word must handle it.
+            R = af_core_target:compile_word("boom", [], [], not_a_list),
+            ?assertMatch({error, _}, R)
+        end}
+    ].

problem_statement:
refactor(errors): normalize error contracts across Util/AgentServer/Storage
## Context
Split from #128 audit umbrella.

## Problem
Error contracts remain inconsistent across `Jido.Util`, `AgentServer`, and storage layers.

## Scope
- Normalize return shapes for validation and runtime errors.
- Standardize not-found semantics to `{:error, :not_found}` for public-facing returns.
- Ensure `Jido.Util` validation errors return `%Jido.Error{}`-compatible tagged tuples.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Contract tests verify normalized error shapes across targeted modules.
- Public APIs avoid bare `:not_found` in favor of `{:error, :not_found}`.
- `mix test`, `mix credo`, and `mix dialyzer` pass.

## Out of Scope
- Introducing a new global error framework.

problem_statement:
Attention control of agent

Right now sensors are wired to agents at startup and stay static. The agent receives whatever the sensor delivers. But what if the agent's current goal or strategy should change what it's paying attention to?

### Additional contract requirements

Jido supports attentional control: while an agent runs, it can dynamically
change what it pays attention to — starting a sensor it was not watching,
replacing or reconfiguring a sensor it already watches, and stopping a sensor
entirely. Plugins can also declare sensor subscriptions, including several
independently tagged instances of the same sensor module. This document defines
the required observable behavior.

## Sensor Lifecycle Directives

- `Jido.Agent.Directive.start_sensor/3` accepts a tag, a sensor module, and an
  optional keyword list of options, and returns a
  `%Jido.Agent.Directive.StartSensor{}` struct with fields `tag`, `sensor`,
  `config`, `meta`, `replace?`, and `link?`.
  Defaults: `config: %{}`, `meta: %{}`, `replace?: true`, `link?: false`.
  The `:config`, `:meta`, `:replace?`, and `:link?` options set the
  corresponding struct fields.
- `Jido.Agent.Directive.stop_sensor/2` accepts a tag and an optional reason
  (default `:normal`) and returns a `%Jido.Agent.Directive.StopSensor{}` struct
  with fields `tag` and `reason`.
- Actions may return these directives together with state updates, like any
  other directive; the owning `Jido.AgentServer` executes them against its own
  runtime.

## StartSensor Execution

- Executing a `StartSensor` directive starts a `Jido.Sensor.Runtime` running
  the given sensor module under the owning agent server and tracks it in the
  agent server's children map under the key `{:sensor, tag}`.
- The tracked child record exposes the sensor module, the `{:sensor, tag}` key,
  the runtime pid, and the `meta` map supplied with the directive.
- The `config` map is validated against the sensor's declared schema. If the
  config does not satisfy the schema, no new sensor runtime is started.
- The runtime context delivered to the sensor includes `:agent_ref` (the
  reference used for signal delivery back to the owner), `:agent_id` (the
  owning agent's id), and `:sensor_tag` (the directive's tag). The sensor can
  observe its validated config and this context through the running runtime.
- Signals emitted by a directive-started sensor are delivered back into the
  owning agent and processed through the agent's normal signal routes.
- If no sensor is currently tracked for the tag and the sensor cannot start —
  for example its config fails schema validation, its `init` returns an error,
  or the given sensor module does not exist — the directive still reports
  success and no child is tracked.

## Replacement Semantics

- If a sensor with the same tag is already running and `replace?` is `true`
  (the default), the new sensor is started and the previous sensor process is
  shut down; afterwards the children map associates the tag with the new
  process and the old process is no longer alive.
- If replacement cannot load the requested sensor module or the new sensor's
  `init` fails, the existing same-tag sensor remains running untouched.
- If `replace?` is `false`, an existing sensor under the same tag is left
  completely untouched (same process, same configuration) and no new sensor is
  started.

## StopSensor Execution

- Executing a `StopSensor` directive for a tracked tag stops the sensor
  runtime with a controlled shutdown whose exit reason is
  `{:shutdown, <given reason>}` and removes the tag from the children map.
- A controlled stop never emits the sensor-exit lifecycle signal (see below).
- Stopping a tag that is not currently tracked is a no-op that succeeds and
  leaves the agent server state unchanged.

## Ownership, Linking, and Lifecycle Signals

- Directive-managed and plugin-subscription sensors are **not** process-linked
  to their owner by default. Their owner is monitored, so an abnormal owner
  exit (including being killed) stops the sensor with exit reason
  `{:owner_down, <owner exit reason>}`. When an agent server is stopped
  normally, all of its managed sensors are also stopped; the shutdown reason
  for that orderly cleanup is not part of the public interface.
- When a tracked sensor exits **unexpectedly**, the owning agent server removes
  it from the children map and delivers a signal of type
  `jido.agent.sensor.exit` to the agent. The signal data includes the sensor's
  `tag`, the exited `pid`, the exit `reason`, the `sensor` module, the `origin`
  (what started it), and a `meta` map. Sensor exits never produce
  `jido.agent.child.exit` signals; that signal type is reserved for child
  agents.
- With `link?: true` the sensor is linked to its owning agent server, so an
  abnormal sensor crash propagates and brings the owning agent server down with
  the sensor's exit reason.
- Even for linked sensors, intentional lifecycle operations stay local: a
  controlled `StopSensor`, or replacement under the same tag, unlinks the old
  sensor before shutting it down, so the owner receives no exit message from
  those operations.

## Standalone Sensor Runtime Start

- In addition to `start_link/1`, `Jido.Sensor.Runtime.start/1` starts a sensor
  runtime with the same options, but not linked to the caller; the caller
  receives no exit message when the runtime stops.
- `start/1` also accepts an `:owner_pid` option. When given, the runtime
  monitors that process and stops with exit reason
  `{:owner_down, <owner exit reason>}` if the owner exits.
- A runtime started without an owner monitor ignores stray `:DOWN` messages and
  keeps running normally.

## Plugin Sensor Subscriptions

- A plugin's `subscriptions/2` callback (and the static `subscriptions:`
  option) may declare each subscription in either of two forms:
  - `{SensorModule, config}` — an untagged subscription. It is tracked in the
    agent server's children map under the key
    `{:sensor, {:plugin, PluginModule, SensorModule}}`, and its sensor-exit
    `tag` is `{:plugin, PluginModule, SensorModule}`.
  - `{tag, SensorModule, config}` — a tagged subscription, tracked under
    `{:sensor, tag}`. Tags allow multiple simultaneous instances of the same
    sensor module (each with its own tag, config, and signals).
- Each declared subscription starts its sensor during agent server
  initialization, and every plugin's subscriptions are started.
- Plugin-subscription sensors are monitored by the agent server (the tracked
  child record holds a monitor reference): when a subscription sensor exits
  unexpectedly, the agent server removes its entry from the children map and
  reports the exit through the `jido.agent.sensor.exit` lifecycle signal
  described above. For plugin subscriptions the sensor-exit `origin` is
  exactly `{:plugin, <plugin module>}`; the exit never produces a
  `jido.agent.child.exit` signal.
- The runtime context delivered to plugin-subscription sensors includes
  `:agent_ref`, `:agent_id`, and `:agent_module`; signals emitted by these
  sensors are delivered to the agent and routed by signal type as usual.

+defmodule Jido.AgentServer.SensorLifecycle do
+  @moduledoc false
+
+  require Logger
+
+  alias Jido.AgentServer
+  alias Jido.AgentServer.{ChildInfo, State}
+  alias Jido.Sensor.Runtime, as: SensorRuntime
+
+  @stop_timeout 5_000
+
+  @spec child_key(term()) :: {:sensor, term()}
+  def child_key(tag), do: {:sensor, tag}
+
+  @spec sensor_child?(ChildInfo.t() | term()) :: boolean()
+  def sensor_child?(%ChildInfo{meta: %{kind: :sensor}}), do: true
+  def sensor_child?(_child), do: false
+
+  @spec start(State.t(), term(), module(), map() | keyword(), map(), keyword()) ::
+          {:ok, State.t()}
+  def start(%State{} = state, tag, sensor, config, meta, opts \\ []) do
+    case validate_sensor_module(sensor) do
+      :ok ->
+        start_validated(state, tag, sensor, config, meta, opts)
+
+      {:error, reason} ->
+        Logger.warning(fn ->
+          "AgentServer #{state.id} cannot start sensor #{inspect(tag)}: #{inspect(reason)}"
+        end)
+
+        {:ok, state}
+    end
+  end
+
+  defp start_validated(state, tag, sensor, config, meta, opts) do
+    replace? = Keyword.get(opts, :replace?, true)
+    key = child_key(tag)
+
+    case State.get_child(state, key) do
+      %ChildInfo{} = child_info ->
+        cond do
+          sensor_child?(child_info) and replace? ->
+            case stop_by_key(state, key, :replace) do
+              {:stopped, state} -> start_new(state, tag, sensor, config, meta, opts)
+              {_result, state} -> {:ok, state}
+            end
+
+          sensor_child?(child_info) ->
+            {:ok, state}
+
+          true ->
+            Logger.warning(fn ->
+              "AgentServer #{state.id} cannot start sensor #{inspect(tag)}: child key already in use"
+            end)
+
+            {:ok, state}
+        end
+
+      nil ->
+        start_new(state, tag, sensor, config, meta, opts)
+    end
+  end
+
+  @spec stop(State.t(), term(), term()) :: {:ok, State.t()}
+  def stop(%State{} = state, tag, reason \\ :normal) do
+    {_result, state} = stop_by_key(state, child_key(tag), reason)
+    {:ok, state}
+  end
+
+  @spec stop_all(State.t(), term()) :: :ok
+  def stop_all(%State{} = state, reason) do
+    Enum.each(state.children, fn {_key, child_info} ->
+      if sensor_child?(child_info) do
+        case stop_child_info(child_info, reason) do
+          :ok ->
+            :ok
+
+          {:error, stop_reason} ->
+            Logger.warning(fn ->
+              "AgentServer #{state.id} failed to stop sensor #{inspect(child_info.tag)} during shutdown: #{inspect(stop_reason)}"
+            end)
+        end
+      end
+    end)
+
+    :ok
+  end
+
+  defp start_new(state, tag, sensor, config, meta, opts) do
+    id = sensor_id(state, tag)
+    origin = Keyword.get(opts, :origin, :directive)
+    link? = Keyword.get(opts, :link?, false) == true
+
+    runtime_opts = [
+      sensor: sensor,
+      config: config,
+      context: sensor_context(state, tag, origin, Keyword.get(opts, :context, %{})),
+      id: id,
+      owner_pid: self()
+    ]
+
+    case start_sensor_runtime(runtime_opts, link?) do
+      {:ok, pid} ->
+        ref = Process.monitor(pid)
+        key = child_key(tag)
+
+        child_info =
+          ChildInfo.new!(%{
+            pid: pid,
+            ref: ref,
+            module: sensor,
+            id: id,
+            partition: state.partition,
+            tag: key,
+            meta: sensor_meta(tag, sensor, config, origin, meta, link?)
+          })
+
+        Logger.debug(fn ->
+          "AgentServer #{state.id} started sensor #{inspect(tag)} with #{inspect(sensor)}"
+        end)
+
+        {:ok, State.add_child(state, key, child_info)}
+
+      {:error, reason} ->
+        Logger.warning(fn ->
+          "AgentServer #{state.id} failed to start sensor #{inspect(tag)} with #{inspect(sensor)}: #{inspect(reason)}"
+        end)
+
+        {:ok, state}
+    end
+  end
+
+  defp validate_sensor_module(sensor) when is_atom(sensor) and not is_nil(sensor) do
+    case Code.ensure_loaded(sensor) do
+      {:module, _module} -> :ok
+      {:error, reason} -> {:error, {:sensor_not_loaded, sensor, reason}}
+    end
+  end
+
+  defp validate_sensor_module(sensor), do: {:error, {:invalid_sensor_module, sensor}}
+
+  defp start_sensor_runtime(runtime_opts, true), do: SensorRuntime.start_link(runtime_opts)
+  defp start_sensor_runtime(runtime_opts, _linked?), do: SensorRuntime.start(runtime_opts)
+
+  defp stop_by_key(state, key, reason) do
+    case State.get_child(state, key) do
+      nil ->
+        Logger.debug(fn ->
+          "AgentServer #{state.id} cannot stop sensor #{inspect(key)}: not found"
+        end)
+
+        {:missing, state}
+
+      %ChildInfo{} = child_info ->
+        if sensor_child?(child_info) do
+          case stop_child_info(child_info, reason) do
+            :ok ->
+              {:stopped, State.remove_child(state, key)}
+
+            {:error, stop_reason} ->
+              Logger.warning(fn ->
+                "AgentServer #{state.id} failed to stop sensor #{inspect(key)}: #{inspect(stop_reason)}"
+              end)
+
+              {:kept, state}
+          end
+        else
+          Logger.warning(fn ->
+            "AgentServer #{state.id} cannot stop sensor #{inspect(key)}: child key is not a sensor"
+          end)
+
+          {:kept, state}
+        end
+    end
+  end
+
+  defp stop_child_info(%ChildInfo{pid: pid, ref: ref} = child_info, reason) do
+    cond do
+      not is_pid(pid) or not Process.alive?(pid) ->
+        demonitor(ref)
+        :ok
+
+      true ->
+        unlinked? = maybe_unlink(child_info)
+
+        case stop_sensor_pid(pid, normalize_stop_reason(reason)) do
+          :ok ->
+            demonitor(ref)
+            :ok
+
+          {:error, _reason} = error ->
+            if Process.alive?(pid) do
+              maybe_relink(child_info, unlinked?)
+              error
+            else
+              demonitor(ref)
+              :ok
+            end
+        end
+    end
+  end
+
+  defp stop_sensor_pid(pid, reason) do
+    GenServer.stop(pid, reason, @stop_timeout)
+  catch
+    :exit, {:noproc, _} ->
+      :ok
+
+    :exit, {:normal, _} ->
+      :ok
+
+    :exit, reason ->
+      {:error, reason}
+  end
+
+  defp demonitor(ref) when is_reference(ref), do: Process.demonitor(ref, [:flush])
+  defp demonitor(_ref), do: false
+
+  defp maybe_unlink(%ChildInfo{pid: pid, meta: %{link?: true}}) when is_pid(pid) do
+    Process.unlink(pid)
+    true
+  end
+
+  defp maybe_unlink(_child_info), do: false
+
+  defp maybe_relink(%ChildInfo{pid: pid}, true) when is_pid(pid) do
+    Process.link(pid)
+  catch
+    :exit, :noproc -> :ok
+  end
+
+  defp maybe_relink(_child_info, _unlinked?), do: :ok
+
+  defp normalize_stop_reason(:normal), do: :normal
+  defp normalize_stop_reason(:shutdown), do: :shutdown
+  defp normalize_stop_reason({:shutdown, _} = reason), do: reason
+  defp normalize_stop_reason(:replace), do: {:shutdown, :replace}
+  defp normalize_stop_reason(reason), do: {:shutdown, reason}
+
+  defp sensor_context(state, tag, origin, extra_context) do
+    base_context = %{
+      agent_ref: AgentServer.via_tuple(state.id, state.registry, partition: state.partition),
+      agent_id: state.id,
+      agent_module: state.agent_module,
+      jido_instance: state.jido,
+      partition: state.partition
+    }
+
+    base_context
+    |> Map.merge(normalize_map(extra_context))
+    |> Map.put(:sensor_tag, tag)
+    |> Map.put(:sensor_origin, origin)
+  end
+
+  defp sensor_meta(tag, sensor, config, origin, meta, link?) do
+    Map.merge(normalize_map(meta), %{
+      kind: :sensor,
+      sensor: sensor,
+      sensor_tag: tag,
+      origin: origin,
+      link?: link?,
+      config_hash: :erlang.phash2(config)
+    })
+  end
+
+  defp normalize_map(value) when is_map(value), do: value
+  defp normalize_map(_value), do: %{}
+
+  defp sensor_id(state, tag) do
+    "#{state.id}/sensor/#{inspect(tag)}"
+  end
+end

+defmodule Jido.AgentServer.Signal.SensorExit do
+  @moduledoc """
+  Emitted when a managed sensor runtime exits unexpectedly.
+
+  Delivered to the owning agent as `jido.agent.sensor.exit` after the sensor has
+  already been removed from the runtime children map. This lets the agent route
+  the lifecycle event to restart, degrade, alert, or ignore without treating the
+  sensor as a child agent.
+
+  ## Fields
+
+  - `:tag` - Agent-local tag assigned to the sensor runtime
+  - `:pid` - PID of the sensor process that exited
+  - `:reason` - Exit reason from the sensor process
+  - `:sensor` - Sensor module that was running
+  - `:origin` - Origin that started the sensor, such as `:directive` or a plugin
+  - `:meta` - Metadata stored with the sensor child info
+  """
+
+  use Jido.Signal,
+    type: "jido.agent.sensor.exit",
+    extension_policy: [
+      {Jido.Signal.Ext.Trace, :optional},
+      {Jido.Signal.Ext.Dispatch, :optional}
+    ],
+    schema: [
+      tag: [type: :any, required: true, doc: "Tag assigned to the sensor runtime"],
+      pid: [type: :any, required: true, doc: "PID of the sensor process that exited"],
+      reason: [type: :any, required: true, doc: "Exit reason from the sensor process"],
+      sensor: [type: :any, required: true, doc: "Sensor module that was running"],
+      origin: [type: :any, required: true, doc: "Origin that started the sensor"],
+      meta: [type: :map, default: %{}, doc: "Metadata stored with the sensor"]
+    ]
+end

problem_statement:
move AI runtime error contract ownership into Jido.AI.Error
## Summary

`jido_ai` has an AI-specific observability surface, but its runtime error contract is still split. Today the effective normalized error envelope is owned largely by `Jido.AI.Signal.Helpers` instead of `Jido.AI.Error`.

## Current gap

- `Jido.AI.Error` is still a thin Splode definition without package-owned `normalize/1`, `to_map/1`, and centralized retryability
- runtime surfaces normalize errors through helper modules rather than a single package-local error adapter
- compatibility matters: existing caller-visible AI error envelopes should stay stable unless an intentional change is documented

## Acceptance criteria

- `Jido.AI.Error` owns normalization, public serialization, and retryability for AI runtime errors
- tool, LLM, and directive runtime paths delegate to `Jido.AI.Error` for error shaping
- `Jido.AI.Signal.Helpers` is reduced to signal-specific helpers instead of owning the package error contract
- tests cover timeouts, supervisor failures, upstream `Jido.Action` / `Jido.Error` values, and plain exceptions
- any caller-visible envelope change is documented clearly

## Related

- Standards doc: https://jido.run/docs/contributors/observability-and-error-reporting-standards
- Related prior branch: #244

### Additional contract requirements

Additional observable requirements for the AI runtime error contract:

Canonical envelope

- The observable AI runtime error contract is the canonical envelope map `%{type, message, details, retryable?}` where `type` is an atom, `message` is a binary, `details` is a JSON-safe map, and `retryable?` is a boolean. Tool, LLM, and directive runtime paths that shape runtime errors produce this envelope shape, and error shaping for these paths goes through `Jido.AI.Error` as the single package-owned adapter. Runtime-path error payloads for a given reason and fallback context match what `Jido.AI.Error.normalize/4` (or `Jido.AI.Error.normalize_result/3` for result tuples) returns for the same inputs.

Normalization

- Result tuples `{:ok, value}` and `{:ok, value, effects}` pass through as `{:ok, value, effects}`; `{:error, reason}` and `{:error, reason, effects}` become `{:error, envelope, effects}` with the envelope produced by normalization of the reason; any other result value is wrapped in a non-retryable envelope of the caller's fallback type and message.
- Maps carrying a `type` (or `code`) plus `message`, with atom or string keys, normalize to that type and message, preserving their `details` map and any explicit retryable flag. Type values given as strings normalize to the corresponding atom type, and non-binary message values normalize to their binary form.
- `Jido.Action`, `Jido.Signal`, and other upstream `Jido`-namespace error structs are normalized through `Jido.Error.to_map/1`.
- Plain exceptions preserve their exception message and use the caller's fallback type, with their struct fields included in `details`.
- The atom `:timeout`, timeout detail tuples, and supervisor start failures normalize to retryable timeout-style envelopes.
- `details` values that contain non-JSON terms (pids, references, tuples, nested improper structures, non-JSON-serializable keys) are sanitized so the resulting envelope is encodable with the project's JSON encoder rather than crashing normalization.

Retryability

- Retryability checks explicit `retryable?`/`retryable` boolean fields first (atom or string keys); an explicit boolean flag always wins over every heuristic below.
- A message carrying the transient-error marker is a retryability heuristic of its own: an envelope whose normalized message is `:transient_error` or the string `"transient_error"` is retryable even when its type alone (for example `:execution_error`) would not be, whether the message was supplied as an atom or a string and whether the envelope used atom or string keys.
- Without an explicit flag or transient-error message, retryability falls back to type-based heuristics (`:timeout`, `:transient`, `:transient_error`, and `:rate_limited` are retryable, with type values accepted as atoms or their string forms) and to truthy retry hints found in `details.retry` (including string-keyed `details` maps; boolean `true` counts as a truthy retry hint).
- A falsy retry hint overrides any retryable type or message heuristic: the envelope is not retryable when `details.retry` is boolean `false`, the string `"false"` (matched after trimming surrounding whitespace and ignoring ASCII case, so values such as `" FALSE "` also count), or the string `"off"`.

Compatibility

- The legacy `Jido.AI.Signal.Helpers` error functions (`error_envelope/4`, `normalize_error/4`, `normalize_result/3`, and `retryable?/1`) remain callable for existing callers and return the same results as the equivalent `Jido.AI.Error` functions for the same inputs. `Jido.AI.Signal.Helpers` otherwise owns only signal-specific concerns (correlation identifiers and stream delta sanitization) and is not the owner of the package runtime error contract.

Serialization

- `Jido.AI.Error.to_map/1` serializes any runtime error term in the canonical envelope shape and returns the same envelope as `Jido.AI.Error.normalize/4` with default fallbacks for that term.

Intentional caller-visible envelope changes

- None. Existing caller-visible error envelopes remain stable.

problem_statement:
[Open agent skills] Specifications drift
We are currently implementing Skills in ZAQ and wanted to evaluate Jido AI's respect to the Open agent skills spec.

It seems some drift exists:

### What Jido AI gets right

**1. Standard data model**

Jido.AI.Skill.Spec represents the standard fields:

* name
* description
* license
* compatibility
* metadata
* allowed tools
* body/source

It adds Jido-specific actions, plugins, versions, tags, and diagnostics, which is fine as an extension.

**2. SKILL.md parsing**

The loader parses YAML frontmatter and Markdown bodies, understands the main standard fields, and supports both strict and lenient modes.

**3. Discovery and precedence**

It scans:

```txt
./.agents/skills/
~/.agents/skills/
```
and gives project skills precedence over user skills, matching the integration guidance.

**4. Correct progressive-disclosure primitive**

Prompt.render_index/2 deliberately excludes bodies and generates a name-and-description catalog with an instruction to call load_skill.

Jido.AI.Actions.Skill.LoadSkill then returns the complete instructions as a tool result only after the model selects a skill. This is the closest match to the recommended Open Agent Skills pattern.

Conceptually:

```txt
SYSTEM
  Base system prompt
  Compact skills index

USER
  Request

ASSISTANT → TOOL
  load_skill(name: "matching-skill")

TOOL RESULT
  Complete skill instructions

ASSISTANT
  Executes the instructions
```

**5. Resource support**

Jido can enumerate scripts/, references/, and assets/ without reading their contents and can load individual resources later. It also includes path-traversal and symlink protections.

### Remaining Jido AI problems

**1. It is opt-in, not automatically integrated**

Jido’s own guide tells consumers to manually:

1. Register the skills.
2. Render the index.
3. Add it to the system prompt.
4. Expose LoadSkill as an agent tool.

That means Jido AI provides the right pieces, but use Jido.AI.Agent does not automatically provide an Open Agent Skills lifecycle.

A developer can also call the older:

```elixir
Skill.Prompt.render(skills)
```

which includes every body by default.

Therefore:

* render_index + load_skill: compatible pattern.
* render over all discovered skills: eager, non-progressive pattern.

**2. Activation tracking is global, not per session**

This is the most material implementation bug.

Jido.AI.Skill.Registry creates one named ETS activation table:

```elixir
@activation_table :jido_skill_activations
```

Entries are keyed only by skill name. There is no agent ID, conversation ID, request ID, or session key.

Consequently, after one agent activates "code-review", every agent using that BEAM runtime sees it as activated. That does not satisfy the documented claim of idempotency “within session.”

The correct key should resemble:

```elixir
{session_id, skill_name}
```

or activation state should live directly in each agent’s Jido.AI.Context.

**3. The model-facing action bypasses the activation subsystem**

Jido.AI.Skill.Activation.activate/1 provides:

* deduplication
* root directory
* resource listing
* activation context

But Jido.AI.Actions.Skill.LoadSkill does not call Activation.activate/1; it directly resolves the registry entry and returns its instructions.

So the actual model-facing path does not benefit from the activation subsystem’s deduplication, resource listing, or root-directory information.

[HIDDEN]
**4. “Durable” does not currently protect conversation context**

The registry can mark an activation as durable, but that appears to affect only whether the ETS entry can be deactivated. The main branch has no runtime consumer connecting this flag to ReAct context compaction.

The Open Agent Skills guide recommends preserving the actual skill content in conversation context, not merely preserving registry metadata.  

**5. Strict validation is not completely strict**

Some specification violations are accepted or modified:

* Directory/name mismatch only produces a warning, even in strict mode.
* Descriptions longer than 1,024 characters are truncated instead of rejected.
* Compatibility longer than 500 characters is truncated.
* Metadata is accepted as any map rather than a string-to-string map.

These are interoperability-friendly choices, but the mode called “strict” is not a strict specification validator.

**6. Discovery lacks bounds and trust controls**

Discovery recursively uses:
```elixir
Path.wildcard("**/SKILL.md")
```

without depth limits, directory-count limits, .gitignore handling, or a project trust gate.

Those controls are recommendations rather than mandatory format requirements, but they matter before using Jido AI with untrusted repositories.

_Jido AI rating_

* Artifact-format support: 0.88
* Progressive-disclosure primitives: 0.92
* Turnkey client implementation: 0.68
* Overall: a solid candidate, but it needs integration and session-scoping fixes

### Additional contract requirements

This task requires turning the Open agent skills support from opt-in pieces into an
automatically integrated, session-scoped, strictly validated subsystem. The following
behaviors are mandatory and observable through public API inputs, outputs, and error
categories.

## Automatic agent integration and initialization timing

- There is a supported way, exposed through `use Jido.AI.Agent`, to attach skill directories
  to an agent (an `agent_skills` macro option accepting a boolean, a list of root
  directories, or a keyword configuration), along with a publicly callable operation that
  prepares the integration from that configuration. A direct path list trusts exactly
  those roots; keyword configurations do not trust roots unless trust is explicitly enabled.
- Preparing the integration with a disabled setting (false or an empty list) succeeds and
  yields an empty result: no specs, an empty index string, no extra tools, and an empty
  tool context map.
- With one or more explicitly trusted root directories, preparation succeeds and yields:
  a spec map keyed by skill name, a progressive-disclosure index string containing each
  skill's name and description but not its body, the skill-loading tool as the single
  additional tool, and a tool-context map that stores the prepared specs under a key
  exposed by the skill-loading action's public `context_skills_key/0` helper.
- When an agent is defined with `agent_skills`, its configured system prompt retains the
  consumer-supplied base instructions and is augmented with the progressive-disclosure
  index (names/descriptions only, never skill bodies); the skill-loading action appears
  in the agent's tool list; and the prepared specs are present in the agent's configured
  base tool context under the key named by `context_skills_key/0`.
- Skill roots are resolved when the agent is initialized (when the instance is created),
  not when its module is compiled: editing a `SKILL.md` between module compilation and
  agent initialization yields the content current at initialization.

## Discovery trust, bounds, and safety

- Explicit root discovery rejects a root whose trust policy is not enabled with
  `{:error, {:untrusted_skill_path, expanded_path}}`.
- Malformed discovery options are rejected without exceptions: non-binary path entries
  yield `{:error, {:invalid_discovery_option, :paths}}`, unsupported trust values yield
  `{:error, {:invalid_discovery_option, :trust}}`, and unknown scope values yield
  `{:error, {:invalid_discovery_option, :scope}}`.
- Discovery enforces scan bounds: a `max_depth` option limits directory nesting (so a
  skill two directory levels below the root is not found at depth 1), and a
  `max_directories` bound fails safely with
  `{:error, {:discovery_limit_exceeded, :max_directories, bound}}` instead of silently
  returning partial results.
- Symlinked `SKILL.md` files are ignored rather than followed outside the trusted root.
- Discovery metadata recorded on specs is a plain string-keyed, string-valued map (for
  example the discovery scope is recorded with a string key and string value).

## Loader strict and lenient validation

- In the default strict mode, specification violations are errors, with each failure
  identifying the field and a reason category:
  - an `allowed-tools` frontmatter list instead of the specification string form yields
    an `:invalid_type` error for the `allowed_tools` field;
  - descriptions longer than 1,024 characters and compatibility strings longer than 500
    characters yield a `:too_long` error for the corresponding field (they are not
    truncated);
  - metadata maps whose keys or values are not both strings yield an `:invalid_metadata`
    error;
  - a non-string license yields an `:invalid_type` error for the `license` field, while
    an explicitly empty-string license remains acceptable;
  - a declared name that differs from the skill's parent directory name yields a
    `directory_name_mismatch` error for the `name` field, and a relative `SKILL.md` path
    is resolved against the current working directory before that parent check.
- In lenient mode the same inputs load successfully with the values normalized to the
  specification types and corresponding warning diagnostics recorded (for example
  warnings typed `invalid_allowed_tools_type`, `invalid_metadata_entries`,
  `invalid_metadata_type`, `invalid_license`, and `directory_name_mismatch`).

## Progressive disclosure prompt defaults

- Rendering a skills prompt omits skill bodies by default; bodies are included only when
  body inclusion is explicitly requested.

## Session-scoped activation and the model-facing load action

- Activation state is scoped by session: the activation subsystem and the registry
  accept an optional `session_id` on activation, query, durability, listing, and
  clearing operations. The same skill name can be activated in two different sessions
  with independent per-session results, is not reported activated in a third session,
  and clearing one session's activations does not affect another session.
- The skill-loading action resolves skills from a scoped catalog stored in the run
  context under `context_skills_key/0` when that key is present, and does not fall
  through from a (possibly empty) scoped catalog to the global registry; a miss in a
  scoped catalog yields the `skill_not_found` error listing only the available names.
- A successful load result always includes `root_dir` (nil when no root is known) and a
  `resources` map with `scripts`, `references`, and `assets` lists alongside the name,
  description, and full instructions.
- Loading through the action activates the skill through the activation subsystem,
  deduplicating within the loader's session (the run context's `agent_id`): the skill is
  activated and reported non-durable for that session and not activated for any other
  session.

## Authentic durable runtime events and compaction

- Runtime execution marks a skill-loading tool-completion event with durable
  skill-activation reference metadata (durable flag, skill-activation kind, and the
  skill name) only when the executed tool is the real skill-loading action; any other
  tool — even one with the same action name — produces no such refs.
- Runtime runtime-event refs carry only authentic provenance; forged durability
  metadata embedded in incoming tool-completed event data is stripped so it cannot make
  non-skill entries durable.
- Context compaction preserves the authentic durable skill-loading tool result and its
  matching assistant tool call. Forged durable markers on unrelated original tool results
  and user entries are removed; an original tool result without a matching assistant tool
  call in the replacement context is not preserved as durable content.

* name
* description
* license
* compatibility
* metadata
* allowed tools
* body/source

It adds Jido-specific actions, plugins, versions, tags, and diagnostics, which is fine as an extension.

**2. SKILL.md parsing**

The loader parses YAML frontmatter and Markdown bodies, understands the main standard fields, and supports both strict and lenient modes.

**3. Discovery and precedence**

It scans:

```txt
./.agents/skills/
~/.agents/skills/
```
and gives project skills precedence over user skills, matching the integration guidance.

**4. Correct progressive-disclosure primitive**

Prompt.render_index/2 deliberately excludes bodies and generates a name-and-description catalog with an instruction to call load_skill.

Jido.AI.Actions.Skill.LoadSkill then returns the complete instructions as a tool result only after the model selects a skill. This is the closest match to the recommended Open Agent Skills pattern.

Conceptually:

```txt
SYSTEM
  Base system prompt
  Compact skills index

USER
  Request

ASSISTANT → TOOL
  load_skill(name: "matching-skill")

TOOL RESULT
  Complete skill instructions

ASSISTANT
  Executes the instructions
```

**5. Resource support**

Jido can enumerate scripts/, references/, and assets/ without reading their contents and can load individual resources later. It also includes path-traversal and symlink protections.

### Remaining Jido AI problems

**1. It is opt-in, not automatically integrated**

Jido’s own guide tells consumers to manually:

1. Register the skills.
2. Render the index.
3. Add it to the system prompt.
4. Expose LoadSkill as an agent tool.

That means Jido AI provides the right pieces, but use Jido.AI.Agent does not automatically provide an Open Agent Skills lifecycle.

A developer can also call the older:

```elixir
Skill.Prompt.render(skills)
```

which includes every body by default.

Therefore:

* render_index + load_skill: compatible pattern.
* render over all discovered skills: eager, non-progressive pattern.

**2. Activation tracking is global, not per session**

This is the most material implementation bug.

Jido.AI.Skill.Registry creates one named ETS activation table:

```elixir
@activation_table :jido_skill_activations
```

Entries are keyed only by skill name. There is no agent ID, conversation ID, request ID, or session key.

Consequently, after one agent activates "code-review", every agent using that BEAM runtime sees it as activated. That does not satisfy the documented claim of idempotency “within session.”

The correct key should resemble:

```elixir
{session_id, skill_name}
```

or activation state should live directly in each agent’s Jido.AI.Context.

**3. The model-facing action bypasses the activation subsystem**

Jido.AI.Skill.Activation.activate/1 provides:

* deduplication
* root directory
* resource listing
* activation context

But Jido.AI.Actions.Skill.LoadSkill does not call Activation.activate/1; it directly resolves the registry entry and returns its instructions.

So the actual model-facing path does not benefit from the activation subsystem’s deduplication, resource listing, or root-directory information.

[HIDDEN]
**4. “Durable” does not currently protect conversation context**

The registry can mark an activation as durable, but that appears to affect only whether the ETS entry can be deactivated. The main branch has no runtime consumer connecting this flag to ReAct context compaction.

The Open Agent Skills guide recommends preserving the actual skill content in conversation context, not merely preserving registry metadata.  

**5. Strict validation is not completely strict**

Some specification violations are accepted or modified:

* Directory/name mismatch only produces a warning, even in strict mode.
* Descriptions longer than 1,024 characters are truncated instead of rejected.
* Compatibility longer than 500 characters is truncated.
* Metadata is accepted as any map rather than a string-to-string map.

These are interoperability-friendly choices, but the mode called “strict” is not a strict specification validator.

**6. Discovery lacks bounds and trust controls**

Discovery recursively uses:
```elixir
Path.wildcard("**/SKILL.md")
```

without depth limits, directory-count limits, .gitignore handling, or a project trust gate.

Those controls are recommendations rather than mandatory format requirements, but they matter before using Jido AI with untrusted repositories.

_Jido AI rating_

* Artifact-format support: 0.88
* Progressive-disclosure primitives: 0.92
* Turnkey client implementation: 0.68
* Overall: a solid candidate, but it needs integration and session-scoping fixes
contract_addendum:
This task requires turning the Open agent skills support from opt-in pieces into an
automatically integrated, session-scoped, strictly validated subsystem. The following
behaviors are mandatory and observable through public API inputs, outputs, and error
categories.

## Automatic agent integration and initialization timing

- There is a supported way, exposed through `use Jido.AI.Agent`, to attach skill directories
  to an agent (an `agent_skills` macro option accepting a boolean, a list of root
  directories, or a keyword configuration), along with a publicly callable operation that
  prepares the integration from that configuration. A direct path list trusts exactly
  those roots; keyword configurations do not trust roots unless trust is explicitly enabled.
- Preparing the integration with a disabled setting (false or an empty list) succeeds and
  yields an empty result: no specs, an empty index string, no extra tools, and an empty
  tool context map.
- With one or more explicitly trusted root directories, preparation succeeds and yields:
  a spec map keyed by skill name, a progressive-disclosure index string containing each
  skill's name and description but not its body, the skill-loading tool as the single
  additional tool, and a tool-context map that stores the prepared specs under a key
  exposed by the skill-loading action's public `context_skills_key/0` helper.
- When an agent is defined with `agent_skills`, its configured system prompt retains the
  consumer-supplied base instructions and is augmented with the progressive-disclosure
  index (names/descriptions only, never skill bodies); the skill-loading action appears
  in the agent's tool list; and the prepared specs are present in the agent's configured
  base tool context under the key named by `context_skills_key/0`.
- Skill roots are resolved when the agent is initialized (when the instance is created),
  not when its module is compiled: editing a `SKILL.md` between module compilation and
  agent initialization yields the content current at initialization.

## Discovery trust, bounds, and safety

- Explicit root discovery rejects a root whose trust policy is not enabled with
  `{:error, {:untrusted_skill_path, expanded_path}}`.
- Malformed discovery options are rejected without exceptions: non-binary path entries
  yield `{:error, {:invalid_discovery_option, :paths}}`, unsupported trust values yield
  `{:error, {:invalid_discovery_option, :trust}}`, and unknown scope values yield
  `{:error, {:invalid_discovery_option, :scope}}`.
- Discovery enforces scan bounds: a `max_depth` option limits directory nesting (so a
  skill two directory levels below the root is not found at depth 1), and a
  `max_directories` bound fails safely with
  `{:error, {:discovery_limit_exceeded, :max_directories, bound}}` instead of silently
  returning partial results.
- Symlinked `SKILL.md` files are ignored rather than followed outside the trusted root.
- Discovery metadata recorded on specs is a plain string-keyed, string-valued map (for
  example the discovery scope is recorded with a string key and string value).

## Loader strict and lenient validation

- In the default strict mode, specification violations are errors, with each failure
  identifying the field and a reason category:
  - an `allowed-tools` frontmatter list instead of the specification string form yields
    an `:invalid_type` error for the `allowed_tools` field;
  - descriptions longer than 1,024 characters and compatibility strings longer than 500
    characters yield a `:too_long` error for the corresponding field (they are not
    truncated);
  - metadata maps whose keys or values are not both strings yield an `:invalid_metadata`
    error;
  - a non-string license yields an `:invalid_type` error for the `license` field, while
    an explicitly empty-string license remains acceptable;
  - a declared name that differs from the skill's parent directory name yields a
    `directory_name_mismatch` error for the `name` field, and a relative `SKILL.md` path
    is resolved against the current working directory before that parent check.
- In lenient mode the same inputs load successfully with the values normalized to the
  specification types and corresponding warning diagnostics recorded (for example
  warnings typed `invalid_allowed_tools_type`, `invalid_metadata_entries`,
  `invalid_metadata_type`, `invalid_license`, and `directory_name_mismatch`).

## Progressive disclosure prompt defaults

- Rendering a skills prompt omits skill bodies by default; bodies are included only when
  body inclusion is explicitly requested.

## Session-scoped activation and the model-facing load action

- Activation state is scoped by session: the activation subsystem and the registry
  accept an optional `session_id` on activation, query, durability, listing, and
  clearing operations. The same skill name can be activated in two different sessions
  with independent per-session results, is not reported activated in a third session,
  and clearing one session's activations does not affect another session.
- The skill-loading action resolves skills from a scoped catalog stored in the run
  context under `context_skills_key/0` when that key is present, and does not fall
  through from a (possibly empty) scoped catalog to the global registry; a miss in a
  scoped catalog yields the `skill_not_found` error listing only the available names.
- A successful load result always includes `root_dir` (nil when no root is known) and a
  `resources` map with `scripts`, `references`, and `assets` lists alongside the name,
  description, and full instructions.
- Loading through the action activates the skill through the activation subsystem,
  deduplicating within the loader's session (the run context's `agent_id`): the skill is
  activated and reported non-durable for that session and not activated for any other
  session.

## Authentic durable runtime events and compaction

- Runtime execution marks a skill-loading tool-completion event with durable
  skill-activation reference metadata (durable flag, skill-activation kind, and the
  skill name) only when the executed tool is the real skill-loading action; any other
  tool — even one with the same action name — produces no such refs.
- Runtime runtime-event refs carry only authentic provenance; forged durability
  metadata embedded in incoming tool-completed event data is stripped so it cannot make
  non-skill entries durable.
- Context compaction preserves the authentic durable skill-loading tool result and its
  matching assistant tool call. Forged durable markers on unrelated original tool results
  and user entries are removed; an original tool result without a matching assistant tool
  call in the replacement context is not preserved as durable content.

+defmodule Jido.AI.Skill.AgentIntegration do
+  @moduledoc """
+  Builds the Agent Skills catalog, loading tool, and reserved tool context for a
+  `Jido.AI.Agent` when the agent instance initializes.
+
+  Discovery is explicit because scanning a project loads instructions from its
+  filesystem. Passing `true` trusts the standard project and user skill roots;
+  passing a list trusts only those roots. Keyword options expose the discovery
+  bounds and a custom trust predicate. Keyword options do not trust any root
+  unless `:trust` is explicitly set.
+  """
+
+  alias Jido.AI.Actions.Skill.LoadSkill
+  alias Jido.AI.Skill.{Discovery, Prompt, Spec}
+
+  @type t :: %{
+          specs: [Spec.t()],
+          index: String.t(),
+          tools: [module()],
+          tool_context: map()
+        }
+
+  @doc """
+  Prepares Agent Skills integration data.
+
+  Accepted values:
+
+  - `false` or `nil` - disable Agent Skills integration
+  - `true` - trust and discover the standard project and user roots
+  - a list of paths - trust and discover only those roots
+  - keyword options - accepts `:paths`, `:trust`, `:max_depth`,
+    `:max_directories`, and `:exclude_directories`
+  """
+  @spec prepare(false | nil | true | [String.t()] | keyword()) :: {:ok, t()} | {:error, term()}
+  def prepare(value \\ false)
+
+  def prepare(value) when value in [false, nil], do: {:ok, empty()}
+
+  def prepare(true), do: prepare(paths: :default, trust: true)
+
+  def prepare([]), do: {:ok, empty()}
+
+  def prepare(paths) when is_list(paths) do
+    cond do
+      Keyword.keyword?(paths) ->
+        prepare_options(paths)
+
+      Enum.all?(paths, &is_binary/1) ->
+        prepare_options(paths: paths, trust: true)
+
+      true ->
+        {:error, {:invalid_agent_skills_option, :paths}}
+    end
+  end
+
+  def prepare(_value), do: {:error, {:invalid_agent_skills_option, :expected_boolean_paths_or_keyword}}
+
+  @doc false
+  @spec prepare!(false | nil | true | [String.t()] | keyword()) :: t()
+  def prepare!(value \\ false) do
+    case prepare(value) do
+      {:ok, integration} -> integration
+      {:error, reason} -> raise ArgumentError, "invalid agent_skills configuration: #{inspect(reason)}"
+    end
+  end
+
+  defp prepare_options(opts) do
+    paths = Keyword.get(opts, :paths, :default)
+
+    discovery_opts =
+      opts
+      |> Keyword.take([:trust, :max_depth, :max_directories, :exclude_directories])
+      |> Keyword.put_new(:trust, false)
+
+    with {:ok, metadata} <- discover(paths, discovery_opts),
+         {:ok, specs} <- load_specs(metadata) do
+      specs = Enum.sort_by(specs, & &1.name)
+
+      {:ok,
+       %{
+         specs: specs,
+         index: Prompt.render_index(specs),
+         tools: if(specs == [], do: [], else: [LoadSkill]),
+         tool_context: %{LoadSkill.context_skills_key() => Map.new(specs, &{&1.name, &1})}
+       }}
+    end
+  end
+
+  defp discover(:default, opts), do: Discovery.discover(opts)
+  defp discover(paths, opts) when is_list(paths), do: Discovery.discover_from(paths, opts)
+  defp discover(_paths, _opts), do: {:error, {:invalid_agent_skills_option, :paths}}
+
+  defp load_specs(metadata) do
+    Enum.reduce_while(metadata, {:ok, []}, fn item, {:ok, specs} ->
+      case Discovery.to_spec(item, lenient: false) do
+        {:ok, spec} -> {:cont, {:ok, [spec | specs]}}
+        {:error, reason} -> {:halt, {:error, {:skill_load_failed, item.skill_md_path, reason}}}
+      end
+    end)
+  end
+
+  defp empty do
+    %{specs: [], index: "", tools: [], tool_context: %{}}
+  end
+end
